moves.spoken: The whole plan with an extra queen is: develop normally first, then open the centre — because in a closed position the queen just sits there doing nothing; only open lines let that material advantage speak. A few running principles from the lesson. When a pawn is attacked, the queen is the worst defender — it's the easiest piece to chase — so defend the pawn with something modest, even a knight to the rim on a3, and keep the queen free. Learn the material threshold: up a queen, shedding a pawn or two to open lines is fine, but giving up a whole piece to open a file is only worth it if you forcibly deliver mate down it — otherwise the open file is a mansion in a ghost town. Treat undefended pieces as the pressure points on the map. And when two of your pieces are attacked at once, run the checklist: can one move to defend the other; if not, can one move away and capture or attack something in return. Then activate the idle pieces and finish with a forced mate.
teaches: open the centre to use the extra queen
the queen is the worst defender
material threshold when up a queen

moves.spoken: After the game, the student explains the plan: a cheeky pre-emptive attack, opening the middle of the board to get the queen working. The instinct was the knight to f5 to prise open the e-file and start pressing.

But here's the correction. Sacrificing a piece to open a file isn't worth it unless you're actively mating on it — the king simply won't stay in the centre, it castles to the other wing, and then the file you opened is worthless, like owning a mansion in a ghost town.
teaches: open lines only mean something with a target

moves.spoken: Developing the bishop early blocked the queen's own natural development. The conventional path is cleaner: bring the knight out to defend and develop, then fight for the centre on the next move.
teaches: do not block your own development

moves.spoken: The right way to open the centre is with d4 and d5 — no rush, complete development first. A push like f4 would have been wrong: it gives up the queen's coverage of h4 and does nothing to control the centre. Once you volunteer to open lines while up a queen, your opponent accepts with open arms and just takes.
teaches: open the centre with pawn breaks, unhurried
